title: The Encampment Stirred and Left You at Dusk or Dawn
intro: Al-Akhtal of Taghlib addressed this ode to the Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan. Al-Marzubani relates that the caliph took the opening departure as a bad omen and turned the word “you” back on his poet. The speaker follows the departing caravan until their paths divide, then brings the whole Euphrates into view to measure the caliph's generosity. His appeal to the dynasty becomes a claim for Taghlib's part in its victories and finally an attack on the tribes of his rivals, including Jarir's own.

translation: The encampment stirred. At dusk or dawn they left you.
A parting full of changes drove them on.
1.sharh: The people who had settled beside him are suddenly on the move. Evening and morning mark the two possible departures. Separation itself seems to have come into camp and driven them out.

translation: The day they were taken from me, I was like a drinker
of wine once held in Homs or Jadar.
2.sharh: Bereavement makes him reel. He gives the wine a provenance in Syria before describing the vessel, so the comparison grows out of the experience of buying and drinking a particular wine.

translation: A brimming jar lined with pitch gave it up,
dark-mottled, the clay crumbling from its spout.
3.sharh: The giver is a pitch-lined jar. Even the seal has a part in the picture. The flakes of dried clay coming off its mouth tell us the vessel has just been opened.

translation: A man who delights in drink, its first fire struck his vitals.
The wine's afterpain scarcely lifted from his heart.
4.sharh: The rush of wine reaches the parts of the body a wound could kill. Its aftermath lingers in the heart, giving the loss an afterlife beyond the first shock.

translation: I was like him, or one whose yearning unstrings
his limbs, or one whose heart a spell has touched.
5.sharh: He tries one likeness after another for the same helplessness. A love that disorders the limbs and a charm working on the heart reach what the account of intoxication has left unsaid.

translation: Out of longing and grief I sent my gaze after them,
their bands on either side of Kawkab.
6.sharh: His eyes alone follow the company. Kawkab fixes the last sight of them on a map, and the separate groups show how far the moving caravan has already stretched.

translation: They urged the mounts on. Their shoulders turned away.
In the litters gazelles answer when you call to them.
7.sharh: The animals are seen from behind. A soft answering call brings the women in their covered litters into view as gazelles, an image that depends as much on sound as on appearance.

translation: They flash a glimpse at men until they steal their wits.
Put their purpose to the test and it wavers.
8.sharh: He likens a momentary display of beauty to a flash. What looks like an invitation to the men proves a poor guarantee of affection, in the judgement of the man left behind.

translation: God confound the love these beauties offer once
they know that age has got the better of you.
9.sharh: The curse falls on the kind of love that vanishes as soon as a man looks old. The speaker who could call to the passing gazelles now imagines how he looks to them.

translation: They turned away when the stringer bent my bow
and the black hair at my shoulders turned white.
10.sharh: His bowed back makes age a bowstringer at work on him. The second sign is visible at a distance, since the hair that falls to his shoulders has changed colour.

translation: They never heed the call of a man in need,
nor does a grey-haired man answer any wish of theirs.
11.sharh: The two halves assign desire to opposite sides. His call expresses a need, while he sees no corresponding wish in the women that might make them turn back.

translation: They went east when the dry wind wrung the branches
and green shoots dried beyond the ploughshare's course.
12.sharh: The wind squeezes moisture from the wood. A narrow strip worked by the plough retains its green, a detail that gives the journey both a direction and a season.

translation: My eye is captive to the water that it pours
over a journey whose people cannot safely meet.
13.sharh: The eye pours out water as though bound to the task. Meeting again would expose the parties to trouble, so the barrier to reunion extends beyond the distance travelled.

translation: Severed as a rope is severed, they go, my gaze following
between al-Shaqiq and the spring of al-Maqsim.
14.sharh: A cut rope gives separation a visible shape. His gaze still spans the ground between two landmarks, doing briefly what the broken tie can no longer do.

translation: They came down along the valley’s flank
to land where Shayban or Ghubar make camp.
15.sharh: The caravan descends into territory identified by the people who pitch their tents there. The tribal names carry the map beyond the last place his eyes could follow.

translation: When they had left al-Qasim to one side and climbed,
or said, “There is the dug trench,”
16.sharh: Their changing angle to al-Qasim marks progress. A landmark comes close enough for someone in the caravan to point it out, but the sentence waits for the next verse to tell us where they stop.

translation: they settled towards evening. We turned our blooded mounts aside.
The time had come for a man with business to travel,
17.sharh: At day's end the women's journey and the speaker's part company. The first-person plural returns with a deliberate turn of the riding camels towards the man who can grant a petition.

translation: to a man whose gifts never pass us by.
God gave him victory. May he have joy of it,
18.sharh: A petitioner introduces the ruler through the gifts that reach him. The verb of victory then comes back as a noun in a blessing, as if the speaker were already offering his congratulations in person.

translation: who wades through the deep, whose omens are blessed,
God's caliph, through whom men pray for rain.
19.sharh: Deep water stands for danger willingly entered. His fortunate bird belongs to the old language of omens, while the prayer for rain places the caliph before God on behalf of his people.

translation: After his inward counsel, resolve stirs him to act
with judgement and two keen sentinels, heart and caution.
20.sharh: A private conversation takes place before a public decision. Heart and caution are given the sharpness of two watchful senses, explaining how the man who enters danger judges it.

translation: The common cause goes steadily forward in his hands.
Once he has made it firm, no hazard takes him unawares.
21.sharh: The subject has widened from his own resolve to the affairs of everyone he governs. Securing a decision is pictured as fastening it against the risk of surprise.

translation: The Euphrates when its feeders surge,
with usher trees along its banks and in midstream,
22.sharh: The river begins a comparison whose answer is held back for three verses. Its feeders pour in until trees usually associated with the bank seem to stand in the middle of the water.

translation: when summer winds buffet it and pools of spray
toss from its swell above the prows,
23.sharh: The word for the boats' prows also means chests. Enough water climbs over them to gather in pools, giving the swollen river a scale we can measure aboard a boat.

translation: rushing headlong from the mountains of the Romans, hidden
by their overhangs and the bends that bar the way,
24.sharh: We follow the river upstream into Byzantine country. The enclosing shoulders of rock hide it from view, so its force seems all the greater when it comes out of the bends.

translation: is never more generous than he when you ask,
nor grander than he when you look him in the face.
25.sharh: Only here does the river meet its match. Its abundance answers to the caliph's generosity and its visible grandeur to the impression he makes when someone stands before him.

translation: Their informer and their schemes kept working on you
till, out of sight, they portioned out their victim's flesh.
26.sharh: Slander takes the form of a gambling slaughter. The absent man supplies the meat and each speaker takes a share, a pointed account of what can be done to a reputation in council.

translation: Whoever folds away his counsel from us,
whose hands grudge us another man's goods,
27.sharh: Advice can be folded up and withheld. The man's hands are also cramped, extraordinarily, over someone else's wealth. He begrudges a gift he would never have to supply himself.

translation: let him be ransom for the Commander of the Faithful
when a grim, hard day bares its back teeth.
28.sharh: The wish weighs the informer against the caliph on a day of battle. The day bares its molars like a beast about to bite, giving the ruler's courage a fitting opponent.

translation: He lays his breast to the ground as a lion does,
waiting for a battle that will leave him prey.
29.sharh: The lion is crouching, its chest against the earth. Its stillness belongs to the moment before the spring, and the casualties of battle already appear to it as slaughtered game.

translation: He brings two hundred thousand forward to a station
where neither jinn nor men have seen their like.
30.sharh: The army enters as an enormous round number. Even the imagined testimony of jinn is enlisted to express the size of the force the caliph can move.

translation: He crosses bridges, building them and pulling them down,
a marked warrior under standards and dust.
31.sharh: A bridge lets his own troops pass and its removal checks pursuit. The work on the crossing brings the vast army into focus around one recognisable figure beneath its standards.

translation: Till battle is joined at al-Taff,
while at al-Thawiyya no bowstring has yet twanged,
32.sharh: The verse places a pitched encounter beside a place where no bow has sounded. One bowstring is enough to register the difference between an army arriving and fighting already under way.

translation: till some men see how far astray they went
and the man with the crooked cheek stands straight.
33.sharh: Proud men turn a cheek aside to avoid facing others. Submission brings the face round, giving a visible consequence to the recognition of error.

translation: He bears Iraq's burdens on his own,
with good once done its people still laid by.
34.sharh: Rule is a weight carried for the people of Iraq. Earlier acts of favour have left a reserve of obligation on which the ruler can draw.

translation: Among a stock of nab' in Quraysh about which men gather,
no tree can stand level with its topmost growth.
35.sharh: Nab' is the tough wood prized for bows. Here the whole tree figures a lineage men gather round, with a crown higher than any neighbouring tree.

translation: It overtops the hills. They dwell at its root,
men of bounty and, when they boast, of honours.
36.sharh: The tree's height goes with an equally secure place at its root. The poet then names what that position means in human terms, a capacity to give and deeds worth recounting.

translation: They rally to the right, spurn foul speech, guard their honour.
When hardship comes upon them, they endure.
37.sharh: Their energy in a public cause goes with restraint in speech. The last clause tests both qualities by asking how the men conduct themselves when trouble actually reaches them.

translation: When darkness settles over every horizon,
they find a way out and a place of refuge.
38.sharh: Trouble darkens the whole horizon. Escape requires two things that the verse names separately, a way through and somewhere to take shelter.

translation: God gave them fortune that brings victory.
Beside it every other fortune is small, of little account.
39.sharh: Good fortune is an active gift that helps them win. Repeating the same word for everyone else's luck makes the difference of degree sound almost like a difference of kind.

translation: They never grew insolent in its possession.
Had it been another people's, they would have exulted.
40.sharh: Their privilege is tested by imagining a change of owners. Another people would have turned success into self-indulgence, in the poet's view.

translation: Wild in enmity until redress is won for them,
the most forbearing of men when they have power.
41.sharh: The opening adjective is used of horses that will suffer no handling. The demand for redress gives way to the freedom to spare once their enemy is in their power.

translation: Men nursing rancour cannot bear the weight of fighting them.
No weakness shows in the wood they spring from.
42.sharh: To take on this war is to lift a weight. Testing their staves for softness recalls the strong tree of their lineage and gives their resistance a physical measure.

translation: They are the men who race the winds
when those who come asking find little food or fall on hard times.
43.sharh: They race the winds to get food to people who come asking. The petitioner might find provisions scarce all around him, or have too little of his own to live on.

translation: Sons of Umayya, your bounty covers all.
It is complete, free of reproach or anything that clouds it.
44.sharh: He turns to the dynasty in person. A gift can reach everyone and still be spoiled afterwards by reminding its recipients what they owe.

translation: Sons of Umayya, I fought in your defence
against sons of men who gave shelter and gave aid.
45.sharh: His weapon in this contest is verse. The two verbs identify the opposing families through their Medinan forebears, who sheltered and supported the Prophet.

translation: I silenced the sons of al-Najjar for you, as
the chiefs of Ma'add know, though long they had roared.
46.sharh: A particular clan now stands for the opposing voices. The noise before their silence is the rumbling of a camel, and the chiefs of Ma'add are invited to act as witnesses.

translation: Till they submitted, still smarting at my words.
Speech goes where needles cannot pierce.
47.sharh: Submission has done nothing to ease the pain. A needle can pierce flesh, but a public verse can reach an injury to honour that has no bodily location.

translation: Sons of Umayya, I offer you counsel.
Never let Zufar pass a night secure among you.
48.sharh: Having claimed a defender's standing, he presumes to advise the court. A night's safety among the Umayyads would signal a degree of trust he resents.

translation: Count him an enemy. What you see of him
and what lies hid of his character are equally vicious.
49.sharh: He claims knowledge of both the visible man and the hidden one. That claim is meant to defeat any sign at court that reconciliation might be genuine.

translation: A grudge, you will find, however old it grows,
is like mange that lies hidden, then spreads.
50.sharh: Mange may disappear from sight before spreading afresh. The apparent interval of health is exactly the interval in which the poet distrusts a former enemy.

translation: Commander of the Faithful, through us you were granted victory
when the news reached you in the heart of the Ghouta.
51.sharh: The speaker claims a share for Taghlib in a victory reported to the caliph near Damascus. That shift from general praise to a named place turns the following description into supposed evidence.

translation: They showed you Ibn al-Hubab's head to recognise,
the sword's mark still on his nose.
52.sharh: Identification makes the trophy serve as proof of the messenger's news. The blade has left a mark on the face the caliph is being asked to recognise.

translation: His ears are stopped. He hears no sound.
He will speak when stone speaks.
53.sharh: A stopped ear might be opened, but the second half makes the condition permanent. The imagined prospect of an answer prepares the cruel address to the head that follows.

translation: His body lay out beside al-Hashshak.
Al-Yahmum and al-Siwar lay between it and his head.
54.sharh: The body stays at the killing ground while the head travels. Naming the country between them turns an itinerary into a measure of bodily separation.

translation: Those of al-Subr from Ghassan, and al-Hazn, ask him there,
“What welcome did the lads out at pasture give you?”
55.sharh: Two Ghassanid groups put a host's question to a head that cannot answer. The language of hospitality makes the jeering reference to the encounter with the herdsmen particularly harsh.

translation: And al-Harith ibn Abi Awf, they tossed him about
till eagles and hawks took their turns over him,
56.sharh: The name brings a second casualty into the boast. Repeated handling on the battlefield gives way to the birds following one another over the body.

translation: and Qays Aylan, until they came riding hard
and pledged you allegiance openly after their denial.
57.sharh: The gait is that of mounts pressed forward. A public oath makes the reversal visible, allowing the poet to present the defeated tribe as witnesses to the caliph's authority.

translation: May God never guide Qays out of their wandering,
nor lift the sons of Dhakwan when they stumble.
58.sharh: A customary wish of recovery is withheld from a man who trips. The smaller group named in the curse is the slain Umayr's own clan.

translation: They cried out when war bit into their shoulders.
Impatience, he says, runs in Qays Aylan.
59.sharh: War bites their withers as though they were riding beasts. By calling their cry impatience, the satirist tries to turn what they suffered into a fault in their character.

translation: They once enjoyed prosperity, till
the devil's snares caught them and they boasted falsely.
60.sharh: For once he concedes that they prospered. The devil's cords tighten as their claims swell, preparing the image of the wretched mount to which they are reduced.

translation: They were flung on an old she-camel, hard to ride,
bare of any tail hair or fleece.
61.sharh: An aged camel with no covering makes a rough seat. The fall from prosperity is felt by the rider's body before it is expressed in political terms.

translation: The course set by its fool so puzzled Sulaym
that it knew neither how to water nor withdraw.
62.sharh: Bringing animals to water and leading them away make up an ordinary day's work. Losing command of both makes political bewilderment intelligible in a herder's terms.

translation: They looked, picking their bitter colocynth,
towards the Zawabi. We spoke once they had looked.
63.sharh: They can see the country they desire while gathering a notoriously bitter fruit. The speaker makes them look first and only then supplies his own side's answer.

translation: They went back to their two lava fields to live there,
as cattle turn back to their familiar ground.
64.sharh: He permits them two old tracts of black stone to inhabit. The comparison with cattle following a habitual track strips their return of the dignity of a military movement.

translation: Sinjar stood empty of them then,
and al-Mahlabiyyat, the Khabur and al-Surar.
65.sharh: A list of places gives their departure a geographical extent. Every new name adds another empty camping ground to the poet's claim for his own people.

translation: They will never match Farras in descent
till the moon meets the Kid beside the northern star.
66.sharh: A genealogical claim is measured against the sky. The moon's path never takes it to the northern stars he names, so the two sides of the comparison can meet only on an impossible day.

translation: Nor al-Dibab when their eyes darken,
nor Usayya, save that they too are human.
67.sharh: More clan names enter the contest over pedigree. At the end of the comparison the satirist grants his opponents just one degree of kinship, their membership of the human race.

translation: No runner of theirs ever strives to catch us
without falling short of us, out of breath.
68.sharh: The genealogy has turned into a footrace. We hear the pursuer gasping, a measure of the effort spent without closing the interval.

translation: Our enmity has already brought down on Kilab
one of those disasters men await in dread.
69.sharh: Kilab supplies a named instance of what enmity with Taghlib can cost. Something only feared or anticipated has already entered the tribe's experience.

translation: The breach has grown beyond all healing.
In it no kinship binds us, no excuse holds.
70.sharh: The vocabulary of a wound that will not knit is applied to a relationship. Neither kinship nor a plea in mitigation can draw its sides together again.

translation: As for Kulayb ibn Yarbu', they have
no going to the waters of honour and no coming back.
71.sharh: Jarir's clan becomes the last large target. Honour has a watering place like the one Sulaym could no longer manage, but Kulayb is denied even the journey to or from it.

translation: Left behind, they let others settle their affairs
in their absence, in the dark, unaware.
72.sharh: Decisions concerning them take place elsewhere. As he tells it, their exclusion is complete enough that they have no idea a decision has even been made.

translation: Slapped at the backs of watering troughs,
they always carry some Darimi's mark.
73.sharh: Access to the trough expresses rank at its most practical. A mark left by a man of Darim is made into evidence that Kulayb must wait its turn.

translation: Wretched sober men, and wretched drinking companions,
once strong drink and date wine run through them.
74.sharh: Sober company and drinking company exhaust the alternatives. The double condemnation leaves them no occasion on which they might show the liberality expected of companions.

translation: A people in whom every indecency comes to rest,
and every shame with which Mudar has been reviled.
75.sharh: The group becomes a collecting place for scandals. He escalates the charge by transferring to a single clan all the disgrace ever imputed to the much larger Mudar.

translation: They jog along on asses. Their disgraces have reached
Najran, or Hajar has had the tale of them.
76.sharh: Their unsoldierly little mounts move slowly. News about them travels considerably faster, crossing the peninsula between towns remote from one another.

translation: They eat poor provisions all alone,
asking from out of sight, “What is the news?”
77.sharh: Eating inferior food alone expresses a meanness deeper than poverty. Their question from the sidelines recalls their absence when others decided their affairs.

translation: Remember Ghudana, a herd of small, ear-tagged
goats, with pens built round them.
78.sharh: Ghudana is another branch of Yarbu'. Little goats with distinguishing tags replace a genealogical portrait, and low enclosures complete the deliberately undignified likeness.

translation: They dribble when the fronts of their shifts grow hot
and huddle up when rain has soaked them.
79.sharh: The crude reference is to sexual fluid at the front of their garments. Heat exposes the body and a shower leaves it shivering, continuing the taunt about a miserable little herd.

translation: What standing has Ghudana anywhere,
these keepers-back of sheep till the dregs are left?
80.sharh: Even at the trough they serve last. The few mouthfuls that other animals leave give a measurable quantity to the small social standing he allows them.

translation: They claim descent from Yarbu', yet their contribution,
when help is pooled, is buried and despised.
81.sharh: They can name an ancestor readily enough. When the contributions to a shared need are laid together, theirs is too small to distinguish.

translation: Their beards yellow from feeding smoky fires, when
winter's cold drives off helpers and stills the milker's hand.
82.sharh: Soot stains mark the men at the fire. When cold checks the milking hand and makes assistance scarce, the poet casts them as servants tending smoke.

translation: Then home again to dark, begrimed women
who never wash, even when their hollows itch.
83.sharh: The return home gives the taunt a last domestic setting. The poet enlists women, skin colour and bodily dirt in an insult meant to disgrace an entire clan.

translation: Glory has sworn in earnest never to ally with them
till hair allies itself with the palm of a hand.
84.sharh: Glory can swear an oath and enter a tribal alliance. The condition it sets is one every listener can check by opening a hand, giving the long quarrel a compact ending.

1.1.2.head: القَطين
1.1.2.meaning: The people settled together in a camp, including their dependants.

1.2.5.head: غِيَر
1.2.5.meaning: Reversals of circumstance. The plural gives separation many turns.

2.2.2.head: قَرقَف
2.2.2.meaning: Qarqaf, a name for wine associated with the shiver it gives its drinker.

2.2.4.head: حِمص
2.2.4.meaning: Homs, the Syrian city named as a possible source of the wine.

2.2.6.head: جَدَر
2.2.6.meaning: Jadar, another Syrian locality associated here with wine. Its precise identification varies.

3.1.4-5.head: ذَوات القار
3.1.4-5.meaning: “The pitch-lined ones”, earthen wine jars sealed with pitch to prevent leaks.

3.2.1.head: كَلفاء
3.2.1.meaning: Dark and mottled, describing the surface of the old wine jar.

3.2.5.head: المَدَر
3.2.5.meaning: Clods of dried clay, here fragments of the seal over the jar's mouth.

4.1.3.head: حُمَيّا
4.1.3.meaning: The first heat or rush of wine as it takes hold.

4.2.6.head: الخُمَر
4.2.6.meaning: After-effects of drinking, especially the headache that outlasts intoxication.

5.1.6.head: خَبَلَ
5.1.6.meaning: Disordered or disabled, here of longing making the limbs fail.

5.2.5.head: النُّشَر
5.2.5.meaning: Nushar, charms or incantations associated with treating someone under a spell.

6.2.3-4.head: جَنَبا كَوكَب
6.2.3-4.meaning: “The two sides of Kawkab”, a place on the caravan's route.

6.2.5.head: زُمَر
6.2.5.meaning: Separate bands of travellers, visible at different points along the route.

7.1.2.head: المَطِيّ
7.1.2.meaning: Riding camels, the mounts bearing the departing company.

7.2.4.head: باغَمَ
7.2.4.meaning: Called softly in imitation of a gazelle's low cry.

7.2.5.head: الصّوَر
7.2.5.meaning: Gazelles turning their necks, a description transferred to the women in litters.

8.1.1.head: أَبرَقَ
8.1.1.meaning: Flash a glimpse of beauty, like a momentary gleam of lightning.

8.1.4.head: اِختَبَلَ
8.1.4.meaning: Steal the onlookers' wits and leave them unable to judge clearly.

9.1.5.head: الغانِيَة
9.1.5.meaning: Beautiful women, conventionally those whose looks require no adornment.

9.2.5.meaning: Overcame or made light of him. Age is the subject of the verb.

10.1.5.head: مُوَتِّر
10.1.5.meaning: A bowstringer, drawing the stave into a curve like the speaker's ageing back.

10.2.4.head: اللِّمَّة
10.2.4.meaning: Hair long enough to fall past the ears towards the shoulders.

11.1.2.head: اِرعَوى
11.1.2.meaning: Turn back or give heed in response to a summons.

11.2.6.head: وَطَر
11.2.6.meaning: A desire or need that draws someone towards another person.

12.1.5.head: بارِح
12.1.5.meaning: A dry summer wind credited here with wringing moisture from the branches.

12.2.3-4.head: مَجرى السِّنَّة
12.2.3-4.meaning: “The course of the blade”, the strip of ground turned by a ploughshare.

13.1.2.head: عانِيَة
13.1.2.meaning: Captive, as though the weeping eye were bound to its tears.

13.2.2.head: نِيَّة
13.2.2.meaning: A destination or projected removal, with the separation that it entails.

14.1.1.head: مُنقَضِب
14.1.1.meaning: Cut off abruptly from those left behind.

14.2.2.head: الشَّقيق
14.2.2.meaning: Al-Shaqiq, a landmark paired with the spring of al-Maqsim.

14.2.3-4.head: عَين المَقسِم
14.2.3-4.meaning: Ayn al-Maqsim, a spring named as a point on the caravan's route.

15.1.5.head: غَضبَة
15.1.5.meaning: A side or flank of a valley. The early scholium compares it with the flank of a camel.

15.2.4.head: شَيبان
15.2.4.meaning: Shayban, a branch of Bakr ibn Wa'il whose camping ground identifies the region.

15.2.6.head: غُبَر
15.2.6.meaning: Ghubar, a group of Bakr ibn Wa'il paired with Shayban.

16.1.4.head: وَرَّكَ
16.1.4.meaning: Put a place off to one side as a traveller does when passing it.

16.1.5.head: القَصيم
16.1.5.meaning: Al-Qasim, a place on this route. The word also denotes sandy ground bearing shrubs.

16.2.5-6.head: الخَندَق الحَفَر
16.2.5-6.meaning: “The dug trench”, identified in the commentaries as Shapur's trench.

17.1.2.head: أُصُل
17.1.2.meaning: In the late afternoon, towards sundown.

17.2.2.meaning: Was timed or awaited until the suitable moment, here of a petitioner's journey.

18.1.4.head: أَعرى
18.1.4.meaning: Pass us over and leave us without a gift, used here under a negative.

18.1.5.head: نافِلَة
18.1.5.meaning: Discretionary gifts bestowed beyond what is owed.

19.1.2.head: الغَمر
19.1.2.meaning: Deep water, an image of danger a brave man enters.

19.1.3-4.head: مَيمون الطّائِر
19.1.3-4.meaning: “Blessed in his bird”, fortunate in his undertakings, from the reading of bird omens.

20.1.3-4.head: نَجِيّ النَّفس
20.1.3-4.meaning: “The soul's private counsel”, the inner conversation that precedes a decision.

20.2.2.head: الأَصمَعان
20.2.2.meaning: The two keen faculties, identified in the verse as heart and caution.

21.2.1.head: اِغتَرَّ
21.2.1.meaning: Catches him unawares after he has secured an affair.

22.1.5.head: حَوالِب
22.1.5.meaning: Feeders swelling the river, also glossed as its surges. The underlying image is of milk flowing.

22.2.5.head: العُشَر
22.2.5.meaning: Ushar, the woody milkweed or calotropis. Floodwater now surrounds it.

23.2.2.head: جُؤجُؤ
23.2.2.meaning: The chests or prows of ships, where they meet the oncoming waves.

23.2.4.head: آذِيّ
23.2.4.meaning: The heavy surge of a body of water, especially its driven waves.

24.1.1.head: مُسحَنفِر
24.1.1.meaning: Rushing headlong with sustained force, here of the Euphrates.

24.2.2.head: أَكافيف
24.2.2.meaning: Projecting margins or shelves of rock enclosing the river's course.

25.2.2.head: أَجهَر
25.2.2.meaning: More imposing to the eye when seen face to face.

25.2.5.head: اِجتَهَرَ
25.2.5.meaning: Is looked upon openly and at close quarters.

26.1.4.head: واشٍ
26.1.4.meaning: An informer who carries malicious tales to someone in power.

26.2.2.head: أَشاطَ
26.2.2.meaning: Destroyed or shed blood, applied to reputations through the image of a slaughtered camel.

26.2.6.head: يَسَرَ
26.2.6.meaning: Divided a slaughtered camel by drawing gambling lots.

27.1.3.head: طاوٍ
27.1.3.meaning: Folding away or withholding the advice he ought to give.

27.2.5.head: حَصَر
27.2.5.meaning: Tightness or niggardliness, even over property belonging to someone else.

28.2.2.head: النَّواجِذ
28.2.2.meaning: The rear teeth, exposed when a mouth opens wide in a snarl.

28.2.4.head: باسِل
28.2.4.meaning: Grim and forbidding, as a face or a day of battle.

29.1.4.head: كَلكَل
29.1.4.meaning: The breast of a lion, pressed low in its crouch.

29.2.5.head: جَزَر
29.2.5.meaning: Slaughter beasts, transferred to the prey expected in battle.

30.1.4.head: مَنزِلَة
30.1.4.meaning: A station or engagement for which troops are brought forward.

31.1.2.head: قَنطَرَة
31.1.2.meaning: Bridges carrying the army across an obstacle.

31.2.4.head: القَتَر
31.2.4.meaning: Dust hanging over an army on the move.

32.1.4.head: الطَّفّ
32.1.4.meaning: Al-Taff, country on the Euphrates in Iraq.

32.2.1.head: الثَّوِيَّة
32.2.1.meaning: Al-Thawiyya, a locality by Kufa, paired with al-Taff.

33.2.5.head: صَعَر
33.2.5.meaning: A sideways twist of cheek or neck associated with hauteur.

34.1.2-3.head: أَثقال العِراق
34.1.2-3.meaning: “Iraq's burdens”, the weight of government and its responsibilities.

34.2.5.head: مُدَّخَر
34.2.5.meaning: Something held in reserve, here the lasting claim created by an earlier favour.

35.1.2.head: نَبعَة
35.1.2.meaning: Nab', a tough bow wood. An individual tree stands for a distinguished lineage.

35.1.5-6.head: عَصَبَ
35.1.5-6.meaning: Gather round and cleave to it, as members of a lineage.

36.1.5.head: أَرومَة
36.1.5.meaning: The rootstock or place of origin, hence the ancestry of a people.

36.2.2.head: الرِّباء
36.2.2.meaning: Increase in bounty, also understood as high standing.

37.1.4-5.meaning: “Men who recoil from foulness”, particularly from obscene or discreditable speech.

37.1.6.head: أُنُف
37.1.6.meaning: Proud in the sense of refusing humiliation and base conduct.

38.1.2.head: تَدَجّى
38.1.2.meaning: Grew densely dark, as when night closes over a place.

38.2.5.head: مُعتَصَر
38.2.5.meaning: A refuge where one may take shelter when pressed.

39.1.3.head: جَدّ
39.1.3.meaning: Good fortune or a share of success bestowed on a person.

40.1.2.head: أَشِرَ
40.1.2.meaning: Grow insolent or wanton through prosperity.

40.1.6.head: مَولى
40.1.6.meaning: Its possessors or masters, the people enjoying the good fortune.

41.1.1.head: شُمُس
41.1.1.meaning: Refractory like horses that resist handling, here in enmity.

41.1.4-5.head: اِستَقادَ
41.1.4-5.meaning: Redress is exacted on their behalf, including the right of retaliation.

42.1.4.head: ضِغن
42.1.4.meaning: Rancours nursed in secret against another.

42.2.5.head: خَوَر
42.2.5.meaning: Weakness or softness, tested here as one might test a wooden stave.

43.2.4.head: عافٍ
43.2.4.meaning: Petitioners who call upon a host for food or material help.

43.2.6.head: قَتَرَ
43.2.6.meaning: Fell into straitened circumstances, with scant food.

44.1.4.head: مُجَلِّلَة
44.1.4.meaning: Enveloping or covering everyone like a garment.

44.2.3.head: مِنَّة
44.2.3.meaning: A reproachful reminder that someone owes you a gift.

45.1.4.head: ناضَلَ
45.1.4.meaning: Fought in defence, originally exchanging shots, here exchanging verse.

45.2.3-6.meaning: “They gave shelter and aid”, identifying the Medinan Ansar through their reception of the Prophet and the emigrants.

46.1.3-4.head: بَنو النَّجّار
46.1.3-4.meaning: Banu al-Najjar, a clan of Khazraj among the Medinan Ansar.

46.2.1-2.head: عُليا مَعَدّ
46.2.1-2.meaning: “The chiefs of Ma'add”, the leading men of the northern Arab lineages.

46.2.5.head: هَدَرَ
46.2.5.meaning: Roared or rumbled like a male camel, applied to boastful voices.

47.1.6.head: مَضَض
47.1.6.meaning: A smart or lingering sting left by what someone has said.

48.2.5.head: زُفَر
48.2.5.meaning: Zufar ibn al-Harith al-Kilabi, the Qaysi leader who came to terms with Abd al-Malik after resisting him.

49.1.4.head: شاهِد
49.1.4.meaning: What is present and observable of a man's conduct.

49.2.5.head: دَعَر
49.2.5.meaning: Viciousness of character, imputed to both public and concealed conduct.

50.2.1.head: العَرّ
50.2.1.meaning: Mange, an infectious skin condition imagined as lying dormant before spreading.

51.2.3-4.head: بَطن الغوطَة
51.2.3-4.meaning: “The heart of the Ghouta”, the irrigated plain around Damascus.

52.1.3-4.head: اِبن الحُباب
52.1.3-4.meaning: Ibn al-Hubab, Umayr of Sulaym, a Qaysi commander killed in the fighting with Taghlib.

52.2.4.head: خَيشوم
52.2.4.meaning: The nose, particularly its upper or inner part, where the blow left its mark.

53.1.4.head: مُستَكّ
53.1.4.meaning: Stopped up, describing ears sealed against sound.

54.1.4.head: الحَشّاك
54.1.4.meaning: Al-Hashshak, a locality near the Khabur where the poem places Umayr's body.

54.2.3-4.head: اليَحموم وَالصِّوَر
54.2.3-4.meaning: Al-Yahmum and al-Siwar, landmarks separating the body from the severed head. Their precise identifications vary.

55.1.2.head: الصُّبر
55.1.2.meaning: Al-Subr, a Ghassanid group paired with al-Hazn, here a proper name.

55.2.3.head: قَرى
55.2.3.meaning: Entertained you as a guest, a bitter inversion addressed to the slain man.

55.2.5.head: الجَشَر
55.2.5.meaning: Herdsmen who take their beasts out to pasture and lodge there with them.

56.1.1-4.head: الحارِث بن أَبي عَوف
56.1.1-4.meaning: Al-Harith ibn Abi Awf, identified by the commentators as a man of Banu Amir ibn Sa'sa'a.

56.2.4.head: السُّبَر
56.2.4.meaning: Smaller birds of prey, distinguished here from eagles.

57.1.1-2.head: قَيس عَيلان
57.1.1-2.meaning: Qays Aylan, a large northern Arab tribal grouping including Sulaym and Kilab.

57.1.5.head: رَقَص
57.1.5.meaning: A jolting, rapid gait of riding camels.

58.2.2.meaning: “Up you get”, a wish for someone who stumbles. The negative withdraws that good wish.

58.2.3-4.head: بَنو ذَكوان
58.2.3-4.meaning: Banu Dhakwan, the branch of Sulaym to which Umayr ibn al-Hubab belonged.

59.1.6.head: غارِب
59.1.6.meaning: Withers, the high point where a camel's neck joins the back in front of the hump.

60.1.3.head: إِمَّة
60.1.3.meaning: A condition of prosperity, with other glosses connecting the word to communal allegiance.

60.2.4.head: اِبتَهَرَ
60.2.4.meaning: Boasted falsely of something they could not claim as their own.

61.1.3.head: شارِف
61.1.3.meaning: An old she-camel past her best as a riding mount.

61.2.1.head: حَصّاء
61.2.1.meaning: Bare of hair or unusually thin-coated.

61.2.4.head: هُلب
61.2.4.meaning: The coarse long hair of an animal's tail.

62.1.3.head: سُلَيم
62.1.3.meaning: Sulaym, a tribe of Qays Aylan and Umayr's own people.

62.2.4-5.head: الإيراد وَالصَّدَر
62.2.4-5.meaning: “Watering and returning”, the paired duties of taking beasts to water and bringing them away.

63.1.5.head: حَنظَل
63.1.5.meaning: Colocynth, a desert gourd celebrated for the bitterness of its fruit.

63.2.2.meaning: Al-Zawabi, the Zabs or their surrounding districts. The precise location intended here is disputed.

64.1.3.head: حَرَّة
64.1.3.meaning: Their two lava fields, tracts of dark volcanic rock.

65.1.3.head: سِنجار
65.1.3.meaning: Sinjar, a town west of Mosul in Upper Mesopotamia.

65.2.1.head: المَحلَبِيّات
65.2.1.meaning: Al-Mahlabiyyat, localities identified in the commentaries with the district of Tall Afar.

65.2.2.head: الخابور
65.2.2.meaning: The Khabur, a tributary of the Euphrates along which there were numerous settlements.

66.1.3.head: فَرّاص
66.1.3.meaning: Farras ibn Ma'n, held up as an exemplar of a lineage his opponents cannot equal.

66.2.3-4.head: جَدي الفَرقَد
66.2.3-4.meaning: “The Kid by the northern star”, circumpolar stars lying outside the moon's track.

67.1.2.head: الضِّباب
67.1.2.meaning: Al-Dibab, a branch of Qays Aylan invoked in the contest over descent.

67.2.2.head: عُصَيَّة
67.2.2.meaning: Usayya, a branch of Sulaym used as a point of comparison.

68.2.5.head: مُنبَهِر
68.2.5.meaning: Out of breath from running hard.

69.1.3.head: كِلاب
69.1.3.meaning: Kilab, a branch of Amir ibn Sa'sa'a and the tribe of Zufar ibn al-Harith.

70.1.5.head: مُلتَئِم
70.1.5.meaning: Knitting together like the edges of a healing wound.

71.1.2-4.head: كُلَيب بن يَربوع
71.1.2-4.meaning: Kulayb ibn Yarbu', the Tamimi clan of Jarir, al-Akhtal's rival in exchanged satires.

71.2.4-6.head: وِرد وَصَدَر
71.2.4-6.meaning: “Going to water and coming away”, transferred to participation in honourable deeds.

72.2.4.head: عَمياء
72.2.4.meaning: A state of blindness or utter uncertainty about what is happening.

73.1.2-3.head: أَعقار الحِياض
73.1.2-3.meaning: “At the backs of the troughs”, away from their privileged approaches.

73.2.3.head: دارِمِيّ
73.2.3.meaning: A Darimi, a man of another branch of Tamim set above Kulayb in this taunt.

74.1.2.head: الصُّحاة
74.1.2.meaning: Sober men, whether still untouched by drink or sober again.

74.2.4.head: المُزّاء
74.2.4.meaning: Muzza', a drink with a tart flavour between sourness and sweetness.

74.2.5.head: السَّكَر
74.2.5.meaning: An intoxicating drink, often understood as fermented dates.

75.2.5.head: مُضَر
75.2.5.meaning: Mudar, the larger northern Arab grouping to which both Tamim and Qays belong.

76.1.2.head: العِيارات
76.1.2.meaning: Asses, the undistinguished mounts in this caricature.

76.2.5.head: هَجَر
76.2.5.meaning: Hajar, an eastern Arabian centre in historical Bahrayn, set against southern Najran.

77.2.2-3.head: ظَهر الغَيب
77.2.2-3.meaning: “From out of sight”, without having attended the gathering where events took place.

78.1.2.head: غُدانَة
78.1.2.meaning: Ghudana, a branch of Yarbu' in Tamim singled out in the closing satire.

78.1.3-4.head: عِدّان مُزَنَّمَة
78.1.3-4.meaning: A herd marked by wattles or tags near the ears, including a cut left for recognition.

78.2.2.head: الحَبَلَّق
78.2.2.meaning: Little or short-legged goats, chosen for the satirist's belittling comparison.

78.2.5.head: الصِّيَر
78.2.5.meaning: Pens built to enclose sheep and goats.

79.1.1.head: أَمذى
79.1.1.meaning: Exudes sexual fluid, a deliberately coarse verb in the taunt.

79.2.1.head: اِزرَأَمَّ
79.2.1.meaning: Contracts or huddles its limbs from cold.

80.2.5.head: سُؤَر
80.2.5.meaning: Dregs or small quantities of water remaining after others have drunk.

81.1.3.head: رِفد
81.1.3.meaning: Their contribution of material help when a common need arises.

82.2.2.head: الرِّفاد
82.2.2.meaning: The helpers or their customary relief, checked in severe winter weather.

82.2.5.head: القِرَر
82.2.5.meaning: Bitter cold, strong enough to stop a hand at the udder.

83.2.6.head: النُّقَر
83.2.6.meaning: Hollows of the body, glossed here as depressions by the hip.

84.2.3-4.head: بَطن الرّاحَة
84.2.3-4.meaning: “The inside of the palm”, the hairless skin that makes the oath impossible to fulfil.
